questions.question: If a student adds water to a concentrated acid quickly, what is likely to happen?

options.text: The solution may splash and cause burns.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The solution may splash and cause burns**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Mixing a concentrated acid with water is a highly **exothermic reaction**, meaning it releases a significant amount of **heat energy**. When water is added to a concentrated acid, the first drop of water reacts with a large excess of acid, generating intense heat locally. ***Hence, the statement "The solution may splash and cause burns" is correct.***
 
• If water is poured into **concentrated sulfuric acid**, the heat generated is so high that it can instantly convert the water into **steam**. This rapid expansion of steam can cause the acid to **splash out** of the container, potentially causing **severe chemical burns** on the skin or eyes of the person performing the experiment.
 
• Acids do not change their physical state to solid upon the addition of water; rather, they become **diluted**. The **solubility** of most common acids like **hydrochloric acid (HCl)** or **sulfuric acid (H2SO4)** increases or remains high in aqueous solutions. ***Hence, the statement "The acid will solidify" is incorrect.***
 
• Because the reaction is **exothermic**, the temperature of the mixture rises sharply. An **endothermic reaction** would be required for the solution to become cold, but the **enthalpy of hydration** for acid molecules is very high and negative. ***Hence, the statement "The solution will become cold" is incorrect.***
 
• Adding water to concentrated acid is never a neutral event; it is a hazardous chemical process that requires strict **safety protocols**. Ignoring the **chemical properties** of concentrated reagents can lead to laboratory accidents and **glassware breakage** due to **thermal shock**. ***Hence, the statement "Nothing will happen" is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Safety Protocol (The AA Rule):** The standard laboratory procedure is to always add **Acid to Aqua (Water)**, never the reverse. By adding **acid slowly** to a large volume of water while **stirring constantly**, the heat generated is distributed throughout the water, which has a **high specific heat capacity**, preventing the mixture from boiling or splashing.
 
• **Specific Heat Capacity:** Water has a high **specific heat capacity** of approximately **4.18 J/g°C**. This property allows it to absorb a significant amount of heat without a drastic increase in temperature, provided the acid is added in small, controlled increments.
 
• **Chemical Burns:** Concentrated acids are **corrosive substances** that can destroy body tissue. **Sulfuric acid** is particularly dangerous because it is also a **strong dehydrating agent**, meaning it removes water molecules from the proteins and lipids in human skin, causing deep **tissue damage**.
 
• **Hydration Energy:** The release of heat occurs because of the formation of **hydronium ions (H3O+)**. The process of **solvating** the acid molecules releases energy that was previously stored in the **chemical bonds**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Protective Gear:** When handling concentrated acids, it is mandatory to wear **Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)**, including **safety goggles**, **lab coats**, and **acid-resistant gloves** to mitigate the risk of accidental splashes.
 
• **Glassware Selection:** It is recommended to use **borosilicate glass** (like Pyrex) for dilutions, as it can withstand the **thermal expansion** caused by the **heat of solution** without cracking.
 
• **First Aid:** In the event of an **acid splash**, the affected area should be flushed immediately with **running water** for at least **15 to 20 minutes** to dilute and remove the chemical, followed by immediate medical consultation.
 
• **Concentration Levels:** A **concentrated acid** typically has a very low water content (e.g., **98% for Sulfuric Acid** or **37% for Hydrochloric Acid**), making the initial contact with water extremely reactive compared to **dilute acids**.

questions.question: Identify the way that is NOT used by insect pests to attack the plants.

options.text: By boring into stem and fruits
By cutting the root, stem and leaf

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**By creeping on stem**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Insect pests** are organisms that cause damage to plants, particularly **agricultural crops**, by feeding on them or transmitting diseases. They generally attack plants in **three** primary ways.
 
• **Cutting the root, stem, and leaf**: Certain insects, known as **chewing insects**, have strong **mandibles** that allow them to bite and cut through various plant parts. Common examples include **caterpillars**, **grasshoppers**, and **locusts**. *Hence, this statement is correct as a method of attack.*
 
• **Boring into stem and fruits**: Many pests, such as **stem borers**, **fruit borers**, and **weevils**, penetrate the internal tissues of the plant. They live and feed inside the plant, often destroying the vascular system or the seeds. *Hence, this statement is correct as a method of attack.*
 
• **Sucking the cell sap**: Pests like **aphids**, **leafhoppers**, and **whiteflies** possess specialized **piercing-sucking mouthparts**. They pierce the plant tissue and suck the **nutrient-rich cell sap** from the **phloem**, causing leaves to curl and plants to wilt. *Hence, this statement is correct as a method of attack.*
 
• **Creeping on stem**: While many insects **creep** or crawl over the plant to reach their feeding site, **creeping** itself is a mode of **locomotion** or movement and not a mechanism for damaging or "attacking" the plant. It does not involve the consumption or destruction of plant tissues. *Hence, this statement is incorrect as a method of attack.*
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is By creeping on stem**.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Plant Damage:**

 
 
• **Chewing Damage**: Identified by missing leaf margins, holes in leaves, or severed stems. **Beetles** and **larvae** are common culprits in **agriculture**.
 
• **Sucking Damage**: Results in **chlorosis** (yellowing), spotting, or stunting of growth. These pests are dangerous because they often act as **vectors** for **viral diseases**.
 
• **Internal Feeding**: **Leaf miners** and **borers** create tunnels within leaves, stems, or fruits, making them difficult to control with contact **insecticides**.
 
 
 
• **Economic Impact:**
 
 
• According to the **Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)**, pests destroy up to **40%** of global crop production annually. This has a direct impact on **food security** and the economy of **developing countries**.
 
• In **India**, significant losses occur in major crops like **paddy**, **cotton**, and **sugarcane** due to specific pests like the **brown plant hopper** and **bollworms**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Pest Management Strategies:**

 
 
• **Integrated Pest Management (IPM)**: A holistic approach that combines **biological**, **cultural**, and **chemical** tools to minimize economic loss while protecting the **environment**.
 
• **Biological Control**: Involves the use of **natural enemies** such as **predators** (e.g., ladybird beetles), **parasitoids** (e.g., Trichogramma), and **pathogens** to manage pest populations.
 
• **Cultural Practices**: Includes **crop rotation**, **intercropping**, and **deep plowing** in the month of **June** or **July** to expose soil-dwelling pests to heat and predators.
 
• **Chemical Control**: The application of **pesticides** such as **malathion** or **chlorpyrifos**. However, over-reliance can lead to **pest resistance** and **bioaccumulation** in the food chain.
 
 
 
• **Defense Mechanisms in Plants:**
 
 
• Plants have evolved **physical defenses** like **thorns**, **spines**, and **thick cuticles** to prevent insects from creeping or biting.
 
• They also produce **chemical defenses** (secondary metabolites) such as **alkaloids**, **tannins**, and **resins** that are toxic or repellent to attacking **insect pests**.

questions.question: The absolute refractive index of a medium is defined as:

options.text: the ratio of speed of light in vacuum to that in medium
the ratio of speed of light in one medium to that in another medium
the ratio of speed of light in medium to that in vacuum
the ratio of speed of light in medium to that in air

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**the ratio of speed of light in vacuum to that in medium**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **absolute refractive index** of a medium is defined as the **ratio** of the **speed of light in a vacuum** (or air) to the **speed of light in the specific medium**. ***Hence, statement A is correct.***
 
• Mathematically, it is represented as **n = c / v**, where **n** is the refractive index, **c** is the speed of light in **vacuum**, and **v** is the speed of light in the **medium**.
 
• The **speed of light in a vacuum** is a fundamental physical constant, approximately **299,792,458 meters per second** (often rounded to **3 x 10⁸ m/s**).
 
• Since it is a ratio of two similar quantities (speeds), the refractive index is a **unitless** and **dimensionless** quantity.
 
• A **higher refractive index** indicates that the speed of light in that medium is **significantly lower** than its speed in a vacuum, making the medium **optically denser**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Relative Refractive Index:** When light travels from one **transparent medium** (Medium 1) to another (Medium 2), the ratio of the speed of light in **Medium 1** to that in **Medium 2** is called the **relative refractive index**. This is different from the absolute index where the first medium is always a **vacuum**.
 
• **Snell's Law:** The refractive index is also related to the **bending of light**. According to **Snell's Law**, the ratio of the **sine of the angle of incidence** (i) to the **sine of the angle of refraction** (r) is equal to the refractive index of the second medium relative to the first.
 
• **Common Refractive Indices:** Different materials have characteristic values. For example, **water** has a refractive index of approximately **1.33**, **crown glass** is around **1.52**, and **diamond** has a very high value of **2.42**.
 
• **Optical Density:** This term refers to the ability of a medium to **refract light**. It should not be confused with **mass density**. An optically denser medium (like **turpentine**) might have a lower mass density than an optically rarer medium (like **water**).
 
• **Factors Affecting Refractive Index:** The value depends on the **nature of the medium**, the **temperature** (as temperature increases, refractive index generally **decreases**), and the **wavelength of light** (dispersion).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **absolute refractive index** of any medium is **always greater than 1** because light travels fastest in a **vacuum**; in any other material, its speed (**v**) is always **less than c**.
 
• The **refractive index of air** is approximately **1.0003**, which is so close to **1** that for most school-level calculations, **air and vacuum** are treated as the same medium.
 
• **Total Internal Reflection:** This phenomenon occurs when light travels from a medium with a **higher refractive index** to one with a **lower refractive index** at an angle greater than the **critical angle**. This is the principle behind **optical fibers**.
 
• **Applications:** Understanding refractive index is essential for designing **eyeglass lenses**, **camera lenses**, **telescopes**, and **microscopes** to ensure light is focused correctly.

questions.question: What causes the acceleration of an object when it falls toward the Earth?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Earth's gravitational force**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **acceleration** of an object falling toward the **Earth** is primarily caused by **Earth's gravitational force**. This force is an attractive pull that the **Earth** exerts on any object with **mass**, drawing it toward its **center**.
 
• According to **Newton's Second Law of Motion**, **acceleration** is produced when a **force** acts on a **mass**. In the context of a falling body, the **unbalanced force** is **gravity**, which results in a constant increase in **velocity** as the object descends.
 
• This specific type of acceleration is known as the **acceleration due to gravity**, represented by the symbol **g**. Near the **surface of the Earth**, its average **numerical value** is approximately **9.8 meters per second squared** (**9.8 m/s²**).
 
• In a **vacuum**, where no other forces like **air resistance** exist, all objects regardless of their **mass** or **shape** will fall with the same **acceleration**. This principle was famously demonstrated by **Galileo Galilei**.
 
• While **air resistance** (Option B) acts on a falling object, it serves to **oppose** the motion rather than cause the **downward acceleration**. **Magnetic force** (Option C) and **Friction** (Option D) are not the fundamental causes of planetary **free fall**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation**: This **law** states that every **particle** in the **universe** attracts every other particle with a **force** that is directly proportional to the product of their **masses** and inversely proportional to the **square of the distance** between their **centers**.
 
• **Mass vs. Weight**: **Mass** is an **intrinsic property** of matter and remains **constant** regardless of **location**. **Weight**, however, is a **force** calculated as the product of **mass** and the **acceleration due to gravity** (**W = m x g**), meaning an object's **weight** changes depending on the **gravitational field strength** of the **planet** it is on.
 
• **Air Resistance and Terminal Velocity**: As an object falls through the **atmosphere**, it collides with **air molecules**, creating **drag**. When the upward **force of air resistance** equals the downward **force of gravity**, the object stops accelerating and falls at a constant speed called **terminal velocity**.
 
• **Free Fall**: A state of **motion** where **gravity** is the **sole force** acting upon an object. **Astronauts** in **orbiting spacecraft** experience a state of **continuous free fall**, which creates the sensation of **weightlessness** or **microgravity**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Variation of g**: The value of **acceleration due to gravity** is not uniform everywhere on **Earth**. It is slightly **higher at the Poles** (approx **9.83 m/s²**) and **lower at the Equator** (approx **9.78 m/s²**) because the **Earth** is an **oblate spheroid**, meaning the **Equator** is further from the **center** than the **Poles**.
 
• **Altitude and Depth**: The value of **g** decreases with an increase in **altitude** (moving away from **Earth**) and also decreases as one goes deeper into the **Earth's crust** toward the **center**.
 
• **Universal Gravitational Constant (G)**: Often confused with **g**, **G** is a **universal constant** with a **value** of **6.674 x 10^-11 Nm²/kg²**, which applies to the **gravitational attraction** between any two **bodies** in the **universe**.
 
• **Vector Quantity**: **Acceleration due to gravity** is a **vector quantity** because it has both **magnitude** and a specific **direction**, which is always **vertically downward** toward the **center of the Earth**.

questions.question: The lens formula is given by:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1/f = 1/v - 1/u**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **lens formula** is a fundamental equation in optics that relates the **focal length (f)** of a lens to the **distance of the object (u)** and the **distance of the image (v)** from the optical center of the lens.
 
• The mathematical expression for this relationship is **1/f = 1/v - 1/u**. ***Hence, statement C is correct.***
 
• Option A suggests **f = v + u**, which implies a simple linear addition of distances that does not account for the refractive properties of a lens. ***Hence, statement A is incorrect.***
 
• Option B presents **f = uv**, suggesting the focal length is a product of distances, which is physically inaccurate for thin lenses. ***Hence, statement B is incorrect.***
 
• Option D mentions **1/f = u/v**, which incorrectly defines the reciprocal of focal length as a ratio of object to image distance. ***Hence, statement D is incorrect.***
 
• This formula is derived for **thin lenses** where the thickness of the lens is negligible compared to the **radii of curvature**. It remains valid for both **convex** and **concave** lenses.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sign Convention**: To use the lens formula correctly, the **New Cartesian Sign Convention** must be applied. The **object distance (u)** is always **negative** as the object is placed to the left. For a **convex lens**, the **focal length (f)** is **positive**, whereas for a **concave lens**, it is **negative**.
 
• **Magnification (m)**: This is the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object. In terms of distance, it is given by **m = v/u**. A **positive magnification** indicates a **virtual and erect** image, while a **negative magnification** indicates a **real and inverted** image.
 
• **Power of a Lens (P)**: The power is defined as the reciprocal of the **focal length** measured in **meters**. The **SI unit** of power is the **Dioptre (D)**. The formula is **P = 1/f (m)**.
 
• **Lens Maker’s Formula**: This formula relates the focal length to the **refractive index (n)** of the material and the **radii of curvature (R1 and R2)** of the two lens surfaces. It is expressed as **1/f = (n - 1) [ (1/R1) - (1/R2) ]**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mirror Formula Comparison**: It is important not to confuse the lens formula with the **mirror formula**, which is **1/f = 1/v + 1/u**. The primary difference is the **positive sign** between the reciprocal distances in mirrors versus the **negative sign** in lenses.
 
• **Real vs. Virtual Images**: In a lens, if **v** is **positive**, the image is formed on the opposite side of the object and is **real**. If **v** is **negative**, the image is on the same side as the object and is **virtual**.
 
• **Historical Development**: The formulation of these optical relationships was significantly advanced by **Carl Friedrich Gauss** in the **19th century**, leading to what is often called **Gaussian Optics**.
 
• **Applications**: The lens formula is essential for calculating dimensions and positions in the design of **spectacles**, **cameras**, **microscopes**, and **astronomical telescopes**. It helps in correcting vision defects like **myopia** (nearsightedness) and **hypermetropia** (farsightedness).

questions.question: Which statement best describes the forces involved when a bird flaps its wings downward to fly upward?

options.text: The bird pushes the air downward, but no equal and opposite force acts on it.
The bird’s weight acts as the action force, and the air provides the reaction force.
The flapping of wings is the action, and the gravity pulling the bird down is the reaction.
The downward push of the wings on the air is the action, and the lift produced by the air on the wings is the reaction.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The downward push of the wings on the air is the action, and the lift produced by the air on the wings is the reaction**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The principle of bird flight is fundamentally based on **Newton's Third Law of Motion**, which states that for every action, there is an **equal and opposite reaction**.
 
• In Statement A, it is claimed that the bird pushes the air downward but no equal and opposite force acts on it. This is scientifically incorrect because **Newton’s Third Law** dictates that forces always exist in pairs. ***Hence, statement A is incorrect.***
 
• In Statement B, the suggestion that the bird’s **weight** acts as the action force and the air provides the reaction is misleading. While weight is the **force of gravity** pulling the bird down, the specific action causing the upward motion is the mechanical push of the wings against the air. ***Hence, statement B is incorrect.***
 
• In Statement C, it is stated that flapping is the action and gravity is the reaction. Gravity is a **non-contact force** exerted by the Earth and is not the reaction to the wing's physical interaction with the air. ***Hence, statement C is incorrect.***
 
• In Statement D, it correctly identifies that when a bird flaps its wings, the **downward push** (the force exerted by the wings on the air) serves as the **action**. Simultaneously, the air exerts an **upward force** (lift) on the wings, which serves as the **reaction**. ***Hence, statement D is correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Newton's Third Law of Motion:** Formulated by **Sir Isaac Newton** in **1687**, this law explains that interaction between two objects results in two forces. These forces are equal in **magnitude** but opposite in **direction**. This law is essential for understanding **aerodynamics** and **propulsion**.
 
• **Mechanics of Flight:** To fly, a bird must overcome its own weight (**gravity**) and the air's resistance (**drag**). It generates **lift** by flapping its wings downward and **thrust** by tilting its wings to push the air backward.
 
• **Applications in Modern Science:** The same principle of action-reaction is used in **Rocket Propulsion**, where the downward expulsion of exhaust gases (**action**) creates an upward thrust (**reaction**) that lifts the rocket into space.
 
• **Aerodynamic Design:** The shape of a bird's wing, known as an **Airfoil**, is curved on top. This design utilizes **Bernoulli's Principle**, where faster-moving air over the top creates **lower pressure**, contributing to the lift generated by the **Newtonian** action-reaction force.
 
• **Examples of Action-Reaction:** Common examples include a **swimmer** pushing the water backward to move forward, the **recoil of a gun** when a bullet is fired, and a person **walking** by pushing the ground backward with their feet.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Force Components:** When the wings flap, the **downstroke** is the primary source of lift. The angle at which the wing meets the air, called the **Angle of Attack**, must be precise to maximize lift and prevent stalling.
 
• **Biological Features:** Birds possess powerful **pectoral muscles** (chest muscles) that provide the necessary **kinetic energy** to perform the action of pushing the air. These muscles can account for up to **25%** of a bird's total body weight.
 
• **Air Density:** The effectiveness of the reaction force depends on **air density**. At higher altitudes, where the air is "thinner" (less dense), birds must flap faster or have a larger **wing surface area** to generate sufficient lift.
 
• **Energy Transfer:** The **work done** by the bird during the downward flap is transferred into **momentum** for the surrounding air and **potential/kinetic energy** for the bird's own body.

questions.question: An electric bulb draws a current of 0.15 { A} for 8 minutes. How much electric charge flows through the circuit during this time?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**72 C**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The relationship between **electric current**, **electric charge**, and **time** is governed by the fundamental formula **Q = I × t**, where **Q** represents the **total charge** in **Coulombs (C)**, **I** represents the **current** in **Amperes (A)**, and **t** represents the **time** in **seconds (s)**.
 
• In this specific numerical problem, the **electric current (I)** drawn by the bulb is given as **0.15 A**. *Hence, the identification of current is correct.*
 
• The **time (t)** for which the current flows is provided as **8 minutes**. Since the **SI unit** for time in this equation must be **seconds**, we perform the conversion: **8 minutes × 60 seconds/minute = 480 seconds**. *Hence, the time conversion is correct.*
 
• By substituting these values into the formula, we calculate the charge: **Q = 0.15 A × 480 s**. This multiplication results in a **numerical value** of **72**. *Hence, the mathematical calculation is correct.*
 
• The **SI unit** of **electric charge** is the **Coulomb (C)**. Therefore, the total charge flowing through the circuit is **72 C**. *Hence, the final derivation of the answer is correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Electric Current:**

 
 
• **Electric current** is defined as the **rate of flow** of electric charges across a cross-section of a conductor. It is a **scalar quantity** even though it has a direction.
 
• The **SI unit** of current is the **Ampere (A)**, named after the **French scientist Andre-Marie Ampere** in the **year 1820**.
 
• **1 Ampere** is constituted by the flow of **1 Coulomb** of charge per **second**.
 
 
 
• **Electric Charge (Q):**
 
 
• The **Coulomb (C)** is the **SI unit** of charge. It is equivalent to the charge contained in nearly **6 × 10^18 electrons**.
 
• The charge of a **single electron** is approximately **1.6 × 10^-19 C**.
 
• Charges are of two types: **positive** (protons) and **negative** (electrons). In a metallic wire, the flow of **electrons** constitutes the current.
 
 
 
• **Measuring Instruments:**
 
 
• An **Ammeter** is a device used to measure **electric current** in a circuit. To ensure **accurate measurement**, it is always connected in **series** because it has **very low internal resistance**.
 
• A **Voltmeter** is used to measure **potential difference** and is connected in **parallel** across the points where the measurement is needed.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Direction of Current:** Conventionally, the direction of **electric current** is taken as opposite to the direction of the flow of **electrons** (which are **negative charges**). It flows from the **positive terminal** to the **negative terminal** of a cell or battery.
 
• **Safety and Circuits:** The **electric bulb** in the question acts as a **resistor**. The **amount of charge** flowing determines the **energy consumed** over time.
 
• **Common Conversions:** In **physics problems**, time is often given in **minutes** or **hours**, but for **Standard units**, it must always be converted to **seconds** before using the **Q = It** formula. For example, **1 hour** equals **3600 seconds**.
 
• **Application of Charge:** The concept of **electric charge** is fundamental in **electrostatics** and **electrodynamics**, used in **applications** ranging from **household appliances** to large-scale **industrial machinery**.

questions.question: Which plant tissue is mostly found in the husk of a coconut, and what is its main function?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sclerenchyma – providing strength and rigidity**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **husk of a coconut** is made up of **sclerenchymatous tissue**. This tissue consists of **dead cells** that are long and narrow, with cell walls heavily thickened due to the deposition of **lignin**.
 
• **Statement A (Collenchyma – providing flexibility)**: This is incorrect. **Collenchyma** is characterized by living cells that are elongated and irregularly thickened at the corners. Its primary function is to provide **flexibility** and **mechanical support**, allowing plant parts like stems and leaves to bend without breaking. *Hence, statement A is incorrect.*
 
• **Statement B (Sclerenchyma – providing strength and rigidity)**: This is correct. **Sclerenchyma** tissue makes the plant part **hard and stiff**. In a coconut, the fibrous **mesocarp** (husk) is composed of these fibers to provide **protection and structural integrity**. *Hence, statement B is correct.*
 
• **Statement C (Parenchyma – storage of food)**: This is incorrect. **Parenchyma** is a simple permanent tissue consisting of relatively unspecialized cells with thin primary walls. Its main functions include **photosynthesis**, **storage of food**, and providing basic support. *Hence, statement C is incorrect.*
 
• **Statement D (Xylem – conducting water and minerals)**: This is incorrect. **Xylem** is a **complex permanent tissue**, not a simple tissue like the others. It is responsible for the **unidirectional transport** of **water and minerals** from the roots to the leaves. *Hence, statement D is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Classification of Plant Tissues**: Plant tissues are broadly divided into **Meristematic tissues** (capable of cell division) and **Permanent tissues** (cells that have lost the ability to divide). Permanent tissues are further divided into **Simple** (one type of cell) and **Complex** (multiple types of cells).
 
• **Simple Permanent Tissues**:
 
 
• **Parenchyma**: Found in the soft parts of plants; can be **Chlorenchyma** (for photosynthesis) or **Aerenchyma** (providing buoyancy in aquatic plants).
 
• **Collenchyma**: Located in the **leaf stalks** (petioles) and below the **epidermis** of dicot stems. It provides **tensile strength**.
 
• **Sclerenchyma**: Provides **rigidity**. Cells are dead at maturity and lack **protoplasm**.
 
 
 
• **Chemical Composition**: The cell walls of **Sclerenchyma** are thickened with **lignin**, a complex **organic polymer** that acts as a waterproof binder. This makes the tissue extremely tough and resistant to environmental degradation, which is why **coconut coir** is used in industrial applications like **ropes and mats**.
 
• **Complex Permanent Tissues**:
 
 
• **Xylem**: Composed of **tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma, and xylem fibers**.
 
• **Phloem**: Composed of **sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, and phloem fibers**; it transports **food (sucrose)** from leaves to other parts.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Lignification**: The process of **lignification** in sclerenchyma cells is so intense that the **internal space (lumen)** of the cell often disappears, leaving a solid **mechanical structure**.
 
• **Biological Significance**: In the **coconut (Cocos nucifera)**, the thick sclerenchymatous husk allows the fruit to **float in seawater** for long distances and protects the embryo from **mechanical damage** during its journey across oceans.
 
• **Types of Sclerenchyma**: It exists in two forms: **Fibers** (long, needle-like cells) and **Sclereids** (short, gritty cells found in the pulp of **pears** or the shells of **walnuts**). The coconut husk is primarily composed of **Sclerenchyma fibers**.

questions.question:
A ball of mass 3 kg is raised to a height of 6 m. Its potential energy is _______.

Take g = 10 { m/s}²
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**180 J**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **potential energy** of an object is the energy possessed by it by virtue of its **position or configuration**. In this specific case, it refers to **gravitational potential energy**, which is the energy an object possesses due to its height above the ground.
 
• The mathematical formula used to calculate gravitational potential energy is **P.E. = m × g × h**, where **m** represents the **mass** of the object, **g** is the **acceleration due to gravity**, and **h** is the **height** or displacement from the reference point.
 
• In the given problem, the **mass (m)** of the ball is **3 kg** and it is raised to a **height (h)** of **6 m**. The value of **acceleration due to gravity (g)** is provided as **10 m/s²**.
 
• By substituting the values into the formula: **P.E. = 3 kg × 10 m/s² × 6 m**. This yields a total of **180**.
 
• The **SI unit** of energy is the **Joule (J)**, named after the English physicist **James Prescott Joule**. Therefore, the calculated potential energy is **180 J**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kinetic Energy (K.E.):** Unlike potential energy, **Kinetic Energy** is the energy possessed by an object due to its **motion**. It is calculated using the formula **K.E. = 1/2 mv²**, where **v** is the **velocity** of the object.
 
• **Mechanical Energy:** The sum total of the **potential energy** and **kinetic energy** of an object is referred to as its total **Mechanical Energy**. According to the **Law of Conservation of Energy**, energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form to another.
 
• **Elastic Potential Energy:** This is another form of potential energy stored as a result of applying a force to deform an elastic object, such as a **compressed spring** or a **stretched rubber band**. The energy is stored until the force is removed and the object returns to its original shape.
 
• **Work-Energy Theorem:** This principle states that the **net work done** on an object is equal to the **change in its kinetic energy**. When work is done to raise an object against gravity, that work is stored as **gravitational potential energy**.
 
• **Units and Dimensions:** Energy has the same **SI unit** as **work**, which is the **Joule**. In terms of base units, **1 Joule** is equal to **1 kg·m²/s²**. The dimensional formula for energy is **[ML²T²]**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mass vs. Weight:** It is important to distinguish between **mass (3 kg)** and **weight**. Weight is a force equal to **mass multiplied by gravity (m × g)**. In this problem, the weight of the ball is **30 Newtons (N)**.
 
• **Reference Level:** Potential energy is always relative to a **reference level** (usually the ground). If the reference level changes, the calculated value of **potential energy** will also change, although the **change in potential energy** remains the same.
 
• **Acceleration due to Gravity:** While **g** is often approximated as **10 m/s²** for calculation ease in competitive exams, its standard value on **Earth** is approximately **9.8 m/s²**. On the **Moon**, the value of **g** is about **1.62 m/s²**, which significantly reduces the potential energy of the same object at the same height.
 
• **Scalar Quantity:** Energy is a **scalar quantity**, meaning it has **magnitude** but no **direction**, unlike force or velocity which are vector quantities.

questions.question: Calcium hydroxide reacts slowly with the carbon dioxide in air to form a thin layer of which compound that could be used for the purpose of whitewashing?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**CaCO3**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Calcium hydroxide**, which is commonly known as **slaked lime** with the chemical formula **Ca(OH)2**, is the primary substance used for **whitewashing** walls.
 
• When a solution of **slaked lime** is applied to the walls, it reacts slowly with the **Carbon dioxide (CO2)** present in the **atmosphere**.
 
• This chemical reaction results in the formation of a thin, hard layer of **Calcium Carbonate (CaCO3)** on the surface of the walls.
 
• The formation of **Calcium Carbonate** usually takes about **2 to 3 days** after the application of the whitewash, providing a **shiny, white finish** to the walls.
 
• The chemical equation for this process is: **Ca(OH)2 (aq) + CO2 (g) → CaCO3 (s) + H2O (l)**. In this reaction, **Calcium hydroxide** combines with **Carbon dioxide** to produce **Calcium carbonate** and **water**.
 
• It is also interesting to note that the chemical formula for **marble** is also **CaCO3**, which explains why the finished wall has a stone-like luster.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Calcium Oxide (CaO):**

 
 
• Also known as **Quicklime** or **burnt lime**, it is a white, caustic, alkaline, crystalline solid at **room temperature**.
 
• When **Quicklime** reacts vigorously with **water**, it produces **slaked lime** (**Calcium hydroxide**), releasing a significant amount of **heat**. This is an **exothermic reaction**.
 
 
 
• **Calcium Bicarbonate (Ca(HCO3)2):**
 
 
• This compound exists only in **aqueous solution**. It is not a solid that can be isolated under standard conditions.
 
• It is formed when **Carbon dioxide** is passed through a solution of **Calcium carbonate** in **water**. It is a major component responsible for **temporary hardness of water**.
 
 
 
• **Calcium Sulfate (CaSO4):**
 
 
• This is a common laboratory and industrial chemical. Its dihydrate form, **CaSO4·2H2O**, is known as **Gypsum**.
 
• The hemihydrate form, **CaSO4·0.5H2O**, is widely known as **Plaster of Paris (POP)**, used in **construction** and **medical casts**.
 
 
 
• **Calcium Carbonate (CaCO3):**
 
 
• Apart from whitewashing, it is found in nature as **limestone**, **chalk**, and **marble**.
 
• It is used extensively in the **cement industry**, **agriculture** (to neutralize acidic soil), and as an **antacid** in **medicine**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Limestone Cycle** describes the industrial transformation of **Calcium carbonate** to **Calcium oxide** via **thermal decomposition** (heating at approximately **900 degrees Celsius**), then to **Calcium hydroxide** via **hydration**, and finally back to **Calcium carbonate** via **carbonation**.
 
• The **carbonation** phase is exactly what occurs during the **whitewashing** process when the wall "dries" and hardens.
 
• **Calcium compounds** are essential in **India** for various industries including **steel manufacturing**, **paper production**, and **sugar refining**.
 
• The **solubility** of **Calcium hydroxide** in **water** is low, and its clear saturated solution is known as **limewater**, used as a standard test for detecting **Carbon dioxide** in **laboratories**.

questions.question: What happens right after the formation and maturation of seeds in flowering plants?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Seed dispersal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The life cycle of a flowering plant follows a specific chronological order: **Pollination**, **Fertilization**, **Seed Formation**, **Seed Dispersal**, and finally **Germination**.
 
• **Seed dispersal** is the process that occurs right after the formation and maturation of seeds. It involves the movement or transport of seeds away from the **parent plant** to ensure the survival of the next generation. ***Hence, the option "Seed dispersal" is the correct sequence.***
 
• **Pollination** is the very first step in the reproductive process, where pollen grains are transferred from the **anther** to the **stigma**. This occurs long before seed maturation. ***Hence, the statement regarding Pollination as the immediate next step is incorrect.***
 
• **Fertilization** occurs after pollination when the male gamete fuses with the female gamete (egg) inside the **ovule**. This process leads to the formation of the **zygote**, which eventually develops into a seed. ***Hence, the statement regarding Fertilization as the immediate next step is incorrect.***
 
• **Seed germination** is the final stage where a seed begins to grow into a **seedling**. However, this can only happen after the seed has been dispersed and finds a suitable environment with adequate **moisture**, **oxygen**, and **temperature**. ***Hence, the statement regarding Seed germination is incorrect as it follows dispersal.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Mechanisms of Seed Dispersal:**

 
 
• **Anemochory (Wind):** Seeds are light or have wing-like structures to fly, such as in **Dandelion** or **Maple** trees.
 
• **Hydrochory (Water):** Fruits or seeds develop floating mechanisms to travel through water bodies, commonly seen in **Coconuts**.
 
• **Zoochory (Animals):** Seeds may have hooks to stick to fur (like **Xanthium**) or are encased in fleshy fruits eaten by animals and birds, later excreted in different **locations**.
 
• **Autochory (Explosion):** Some plants, like **Peas** or **Balsam**, have pods that burst open with force, scattering seeds away from the plant.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Dispersal:**
 
 
• It prevents **overcrowding** around the parent plant, which reduces competition for **sunlight**, **water**, and **soil minerals**.
 
• It allows the species to invade and **colonize** new **habitats**, increasing the chances of survival against localized environmental threats.
 
 
 
• **Seed Anatomy:**
 
 
• A mature seed consists of an **Embryo** (the future plant), **Endosperm** (food storage), and a protective **Seed Coat** (testa).
 
• In **Angiosperms** (flowering plants), seeds are protected inside a **fruit**, which develops from the **ovary** after fertilization.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Double Fertilization:** A unique feature of flowering plants where one male gamete fuses with the egg to form a **2n Zygote**, and another fuses with two polar nuclei to form a **3n Endosperm**.
 
• **Dormancy:** After maturation and dispersal, many seeds enter a period of **metabolic inactivity** called **dormancy**. This allows them to survive **unfavorable conditions** like extreme cold or drought for **months** or even **years**.
 
• **Germination Requirements:** For a dispersed seed to germinate, it typically requires a **water** uptake (imbibition), optimal **temperature** (usually between **25°C to 30°C**), and **oxygen** for cellular respiration.

questions.question: What happens when you dissolve sugar in water?

options.text: Sugar particles occupy spaces between water particles
Particles of sugar settle at the bottom

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sugar particles occupy spaces between water particles**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to the **Particulate Nature of Matter**, all matter is made up of extremely small **particles**. In a liquid like **water**, these particles are not as tightly packed as in solids and have small **intermolecular spaces** between them.
 
• When **sugar** (the **solute**) is added to **water** (the **solvent**), the sugar crystals break down into individual **molecules** or **particles**. These tiny particles move into the empty **spaces** present between the water particles. ***Hence, statement A is correct.***
 
• The process of sugar dissolving in water is a **physical change** rather than a chemical one. Under normal conditions, sugar does not chemically **react** with water to form a new substance; it simply forms a **mixture**. ***Hence, statement B is incorrect.***
 
• **Evaporation** is the process where a liquid changes into **vapor**. While water can be evaporated to recover the sugar, the act of **dissolving** sugar itself does not cause the water to evaporate. ***Hence, statement C is incorrect.***
 
• When a substance is **soluble**, its particles distribute **uniformly** throughout the liquid. If the sugar is not in excess (below the **saturation point**), the particles will not **settle** at the bottom but will remain suspended in a **homogeneous mixture**. ***Hence, statement D is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Solubility and Temperature:** The **solubility** of solids like sugar generally **increases** with an increase in **temperature**. When water is heated, the **kinetic energy** of the water particles increases, causing them to move more vigorously and creating larger **spaces** for sugar particles to occupy.
 
• **Saturated vs. Unsaturated Solutions:** An **unsaturated solution** is one that can dissolve more solute at a given temperature. A **saturated solution** is reached when no more sugar can occupy the spaces between the water particles at that specific **temperature** and **pressure**.
 
• **Homogeneous Mixture:** A sugar-water solution is a **homogeneous mixture**, also known as a **true solution**. This means the **composition** and properties are uniform throughout the entire **volume** of the liquid.
 
• **Concentration:** The amount of sugar dissolved in a specific volume of water determines the **concentration**. This can be expressed in various units such as **molarity**, **molality**, or **mass percentage**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Law of Conservation of Mass:** During the dissolution process, the **total mass** of the solution is equal to the sum of the mass of the **sugar** and the mass of the **water**. For **example**, if **10 grams** of sugar are dissolved in **100 grams** of water, the final solution will weigh **110 grams**.
 
• **Volume Observation:** Interestingly, when a small amount of sugar is dissolved in water, the **volume** of the water does not increase significantly. This is a direct **experimental proof** that matter is made of particles and that there are **voids** or spaces between them.
 
• **Diffusion:** The spread of sugar particles throughout the water without stirring is due to **diffusion**, which is the movement of particles from a region of **higher concentration** to a region of **lower concentration**.
 
• **Physical Recovery:** Because dissolving is a **physical process**, the sugar can be reclaimed through **crystallization** or **distillation**, where the water is removed, leaving the **solute** behind.

questions.question: The approximate radii of hydrogen atom is:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**10⁻¹⁰ m**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **radius of a hydrogen atom** is approximately **10⁻¹⁰ meters**. In the field of atomic physics, this specific length scale is also known as **1 Angstrom (Å)**.
 
• More precisely, the **Bohr radius**, which represents the most probable distance between the nucleus and the electron in a **hydrogen atom** in its **ground state**, is calculated to be **0.529 × 10⁻¹⁰ m** (or **0.529 Å**).
 
• The concept of atomic radii was significantly advanced by **Niels Bohr** in the **year 1913** when he proposed his **atomic model**, which successfully explained the spectral lines of **hydrogen**.
 
• A **hydrogen atom** consists of a single **proton** in the **nucleus** and a single **electron** orbiting it. Due to this simple structure, it serves as the fundamental unit for measuring **atomic sizes** in **chemistry** and **physics**.
 
• While the **atom** itself is about **10⁻¹⁰ m** in size, the **nucleus** at its center is significantly smaller, with a **radius** of approximately **10⁻¹⁵ m**, often referred to as a **fermi** or **femtometer**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Units of Measurement:** Atomic dimensions are typically expressed in **nanometers (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m)**, **picometers (1 pm = 10⁻¹² m)**, or **Angstroms (1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m)**. For example, the radius of a **hydrogen atom** is roughly **0.053 nm** or **53 pm**.
 
• **Scale Comparison:** To visualize the **scale**, if an **atom** were expanded to the size of a **football stadium**, the **nucleus** would be roughly the size of a **small marble** placed in the center, highlighting that **atoms** are mostly **empty space**.
 
• **Periodic Table Trends:** The **atomic radius** generally **increases** as you move **down a group** in the **periodic table** due to the addition of **new energy shells**. Conversely, it **decreases** across a **period** from **left to right** because the **effective nuclear charge** increases, pulling **electrons** closer to the **nucleus**.
 
• **Applications:** Understanding the **size of atoms** is crucial in **nanotechnology**, **molecular biology**, and **material science**, as it determines how **atoms** bond and interact to form **molecules**.
 
• **Discovery Context:** **Ernest Rutherford** conducted his famous **gold foil experiment** in **1911**, which led to the discovery of the **nucleus** and established the **nuclear model** of the **atom**, preceding **Bohr’s** refinements.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Atomic Volume:** The **volume** of an **atom** is determined by the **electron cloud**. Since **hydrogen** is the **lightest element** with the **atomic number 1**, it has the **smallest atomic radius** among non-noble gas elements in its neutral state.
 
• **Quantum Mechanics:** In modern **quantum mechanics**, the **electron** does not move in a fixed circular path but exists in an **orbital** or a **probability cloud**. The value **10⁻¹⁰ m** represents the **average distance** or the boundary within which the **electron** is likely to be found.
 
• **Bond Lengths:** The **atomic radius** is often used to calculate **covalent bond lengths**. For a **hydrogen molecule (H₂)**, the **bond length** is approximately **0.74 Å**, which is less than the sum of two **atomic radii** due to **orbital overlap**.
 
• **Scientific Constants:** The **Bohr radius (a₀)** is a **physical constant** used in **Schrödinger's equation** and is approximately **5.29177 × 10⁻¹¹ meters**.

questions.question: Which of the following contraceptive devices/methods prevent(s) spreading of STDs (Sexually Transmitted Diseases) such as AIDS?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Condoms**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Condoms** are highly effective **barrier methods** of contraception that serve a dual purpose: preventing **unwanted pregnancy** and reducing the transmission of **Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STDs)**.
 
• They act as a physical **barrier** that prevents the **exchange of bodily fluids** (such as semen, vaginal secretions, or blood) during **sexual intercourse**, which is the primary mode of transmission for many **pathogens**.
 
• Condoms are the only contraceptive method that provides significant protection against **HIV/AIDS**, **Gonorrhea**, **Syphilis**, **Chlamydia**, and **Trichomoniasis** by covering the **mucosal surfaces** and preventing direct contact. *Hence, the statement regarding Condoms is correct.*
 
• Most condoms are made of **Latex**, though alternatives like **Polyurethane** or **Polyisoprene** are available for individuals with **latex allergies**.
 
• When used **consistently and correctly**, condoms have a very high **efficacy rate** in preventing both **conception** and the spread of **infections**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Vasectomy and Tubectomy:**

 
 
• These are **permanent surgical methods** of sterilization. **Vasectomy** involves the cutting or tying of the **vas deferens** in **males**, while **Tubectomy** involves the blocking or cutting of the **fallopian tubes** in **females**.
 
• While they are nearly **100% effective** for **birth control**, they do not prevent the exchange of **fluids** or skin-to-skin contact, meaning they offer **no protection** against **STDs**. *Hence, the statement regarding Vasectomy/Tubectomy is incorrect.*
 
 
 
• **Oral Contraceptive Pills:**
 
 
• These are **hormonal methods** that usually contain a combination of **Estrogen** and **Progestogen** or progestogen alone. They work by preventing **ovulation** (the release of an egg).
 
• These pills must be taken **daily** for **21 days** of a menstrual cycle. While effective at preventing **pregnancy**, they do not provide a **physical barrier** and thus cannot stop the spread of **STDs**. *Hence, the statement regarding Oral Pills is incorrect.*
 
 
 
• **Copper T (IUD):**
 
 
• The **Copper T** is an **Intrauterine Device (IUD)** inserted into the **uterus** by a medical professional. It releases **copper ions** that are **spermicidal**, suppressing **sperm motility** and **fertilizing capacity**.
 
• It is a **long-term** reversible contraceptive that can last for **3 to 10 years**. However, because it is located inside the **uterus**, it does not prevent **infections** transmitted through the **vagina** or external genitalia. *Hence, the statement regarding Copper T is incorrect.*
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome):** It is a life-threatening condition caused by the **Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)**. HIV destroys the **immune system** (specifically **CD4 T-cells**), making the body vulnerable to **opportunistic infections**.
 
• **STDs/STIs:** These are infections primarily passed through **sexual contact**. Examples include **Genital Herpes**, **Hepatitis B**, and **Human Papillomavirus (HPV)**. While **vaccines** exist for **Hepatitis B** and **HPV**, barrier methods remain the first line of defense during **sexual activity**.
 
• **Failure Rates:** The **typical use failure rate** for male condoms is approximately **13%**, but with **perfect use**, the failure rate drops to about **2%**. Failure usually occurs due to **slippage**, **breakage**, or **incorrect application**.
 
• **Public Health Initiatives:** The **National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO)** in **India**, established in **1992**, promotes the use of **condoms** as a key strategy to achieve the goal of **Zero new HIV infections**.

questions.question: If the time period of a sound wave is T , what does 1/T represent?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Frequency**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Frequency** is defined as the number of complete oscillations or cycles a sound wave makes per unit of **time**. It is represented by the Greek letter **nu** or simply **f**.
 
• The relationship between the **Time Period (T)** and **Frequency** is reciprocal. If **T** is the time taken for one full vibration, then the number of vibrations in one second is **1/T**. ***Hence, the statement that 1/T represents Frequency is correct.***
 
• The **SI unit** of frequency is the **Hertz (Hz)**. This unit is named in honor of **Heinrich Rudolf Hertz**, a famous **German physicist** who proved the existence of electromagnetic waves in the late **19th century**.
 
• A frequency of **1 Hz** means that **one cycle** occurs per **second**. If the time period of a wave decreases, its frequency increases proportionally, indicating more vibrations occur within the same **time interval**.
 
• **Frequency** determines the **pitch** of a sound. A **high-frequency** wave produces a high-pitched sound (like a whistle), while a **low-frequency** wave produces a low-pitched sound (like a drum).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Time Period (T):**

 
 
• The **Time Period** is the time required for one complete **oscillation** of the density of the medium to-and-fro.
 
• Its **SI unit** is the **second (s)**. It is the time taken by two consecutive **compressions** or **rarefactions** to cross a fixed point.
 
 
 
• **Wavelength:**
 
 
• **Wavelength** is the physical distance between two consecutive identical parts of a wave, such as the distance between two **crests** or two **compressions**.
 
• It is commonly denoted by the Greek letter **Lambda** and its **SI unit** is the **meter (m)**.
 
 
 
• **Amplitude (A):**
 
 
• **Amplitude** represents the maximum **displacement** of the particles of the medium from their original mean position on either side.
 
• It determines the **loudness** or **intensity** of the sound. Larger amplitude results in a **louder** sound.
 
 
 
• **Speed of Sound (v):**
 
 
• The **Speed** of a wave is the distance it travels per unit **time**. It is calculated using the formula: **Speed = Frequency x Wavelength**.
 
• The speed of sound varies depending on the **medium** (solid, liquid, or gas) and **temperature**. For instance, in **dry air** at **20 degrees Celsius**, the speed is approximately **343 meters per second**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Human Audibility Range:** The average human ear can perceive sounds with frequencies ranging from **20 Hz** to **20,000 Hz (20 kHz)**.
 
• **Infrasonic Sound:** Sounds with a frequency lower than **20 Hz** are termed **infrasonic**. These are often produced by large objects like **elephants**, **whales**, or **seismic waves** during earthquakes.
 
• **Ultrasonic Sound:** Frequencies higher than **20,000 Hz** are called **ultrasonic**. These are used in various **medical applications** like **echocardiography** and **ultrasound imaging**, as well as by animals like **bats** for navigation.
 
• **Constant Frequency:** When a sound wave moves from one **medium** to another (e.g., from air to water), its **frequency** remains **constant** because it depends on the **source**, but its **speed** and **wavelength** change.

questions.question: The ________ is the longest cell in the human body.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**neuron**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **neuron**, also known as a **nerve cell**, is the fundamental building block of the **nervous system**. It is specialized to transmit information to other nerve cells, muscle, or gland cells.
 
• In the human body, the **neuron** is the **longest cell**. Some neurons, such as the **motor neurons** that extend from the base of the **spinal cord** to the **muscles of the foot**, can reach a length of up to **1 meter (approx. 3.3 feet)** or more. ***Hence, the option identifying the neuron as the longest cell is correct.***
 
• The extreme length of a neuron is primarily due to its **Axon**. The axon is a long, slender projection that conducts **electrical impulses** (action potentials) away from the cell body (soma).
 
• Neurons consist of three main parts: the **Cell Body (Soma)**, which contains the **nucleus**; **Dendrites**, which receive signals; and the **Axon**, which transmits signals. The presence of the **Myelin sheath** around many axons allows for rapid signal conduction over these long distances.
 
• Unlike many other cells in the body, mature neurons in the **Central Nervous System (CNS)** generally do not undergo **cell division** (mitosis), meaning they are often as **old** as the individual.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Muscle Fibre:**

 
 
• **Muscle fibres** (specifically skeletal muscle cells) are also quite long and are **multinucleated**.
 
• While they can reach lengths of up to **30 cm** in the **Sartorius muscle** of the thigh, they are generally shorter than the longest neurons. ***Hence, this statement is not the primary answer regarding the longest cell.***
 
• Their main **function** is **contraction** to facilitate movement, powered by proteins like **actin** and **myosin**.
 
 
 
• **Platelet (Thrombocyte):**
 
 
• **Platelets** are not complete cells but rather **cell fragments** derived from **megakaryocytes** in the **bone marrow**.
 
• They are very small, typically **2 to 3 micrometers** in diameter, and lack a **nucleus**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect as they are among the smallest components in the blood.***
 
• Their primary **application** is in **blood clotting** (hemostasis) and wound healing.
 
 
 
• **Osteocyte:**
 
 
• An **osteocyte** is a **mature bone cell** that resides within the **lacunae** of the bone matrix.
 
• They are involved in the **maintenance of bone tissue** and respond to **mechanical strain**. ***Hence, this statement is incorrect in the context of being the longest cell.***
 
• They develop from **osteoblasts** and remain embedded in the **calcified matrix** they helped create.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Largest Cell in Humans:** While the neuron is the **longest**, the **human ovum (egg cell)** is considered the **largest cell** in terms of **volume and diameter** (roughly **120 to 150 micrometers**), making it visible to the **naked eye**.
 
• **Smallest Cell in Humans:** The **Sperm cell** is often cited as the **smallest cell** in terms of volume, although the **cerebellum granule cell** is also a candidate for the smallest based on size.
 
• **Nervous System Location:** Neurons are found throughout the **Brain**, **Spinal Cord**, and the **Peripheral Nervous System**.
 
• **Data on Synapses:** A single neuron can have thousands of **synaptic connections** with other neurons, forming complex **neural networks** that process **sensory data** and coordinate **motor functions**.

questions.question: Substances that are broken down by biological processes are said to be:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Biodegradable**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Biodegradable** substances are materials that can be broken down or decomposed into simpler, harmless substances by the action of **microorganisms** such as **bacteria**, **fungi**, and **earthworms**.
 
• The process through which these substances are decomposed is known as **biodegradation**. This is a **biological process** where complex **organic matter** is converted into **carbon dioxide**, **water**, and **biomass**.
 
• These substances are typically **natural materials**. Common examples include **vegetable peels**, **fruits**, **paper**, **cotton**, **wool**, **wood**, and **animal waste**.
 
• Since these materials return to the **soil** and become part of the **nutrient cycle**, they do not cause long-term **environmental pollution**. Hence, the substances broken down by biological processes are called biodegradable.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Non-biodegradable**: These are substances that cannot be broken down by **biological processes** or the action of **microbes**. They persist in the **environment** for a very long time, often for **hundreds of years**. Examples include **plastics**, **polythene bags**, and **DDT**. Their accumulation leads to **soil pollution** and **clogging of drainage systems**.
 
• **Synthetic**: These are **man-made** materials produced through **chemical synthesis** in **industries**. While some modern synthetic materials are designed to be **bio-plastics**, most traditional **synthetic fibers** like **nylon**, **polyester**, and **acrylic** are **non-biodegradable** and resistant to **natural decay**.
 
• **Metallic**: This category includes **elements** or **alloys** like **iron**, **aluminum**, **copper**, and **lead**. While metals may undergo **chemical oxidation** (like **rusting** of iron), they are not broken down by **biological enzymes** or **microorganisms**, making them **non-biodegradable** in a biological context.
 
• **Biomagnification**: This is a **functional** consequence of **non-biodegradable** substances. Chemicals like **mercury** or **pesticides** (e.g., **DDT**) enter the **food chain** and increase in **concentration** at each **trophic level**, posing a **health risk** to **apex predators** and **humans**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Decomposers**: These are the **saprophytic organisms** that play a vital **function** in the **ecosystem** by breaking down **dead organic matter**. Without them, the **earth** would be covered in **waste** and **nutrients** would not be recycled.
 
• **Factors affecting Biodegradation**: The **rate** at which a substance decomposes depends on **environmental factors** such as **temperature**, **moisture**, **oxygen availability**, and **pH levels**. For example, **aerobic decomposition** occurs faster in the presence of **oxygen** compared to **anaerobic** conditions.
 
• **Waste Management**: To protect the **environment**, it is crucial to segregate **waste** at the source into **dry waste** (non-biodegradable) and **wet waste** (biodegradable). Biodegradable waste can be converted into **manure** or **compost** through **composting** or **vermicomposting** (using **red worms**).

 Work done in 4 days Remaining Work 10 Women 30 Women (10 + 20)

questions.question: A train overtakes two people running along a railway track. The first person is running at 12.6 km/hr, and the second person is running at 25.2 km/hr. If 3 is added to the numerator of a fraction, it becomes 1, and if 4 is added to the denominator of the fraction, it becomes (4)/(5) .

Condition 2: N / (D + 4) = 4/5 ⇒ 5N = 4D + 16

Substitute D = N + 3 into the second condition: 5N = 4(N + 3) + 16

5N = 4N + 12 + 16 ⇒ N = 28

Denominator D = 28 + 3 = 31

**∴ Answer = 868**

questions.question: The Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025, is also known as __________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**UMEED Act**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Waqf (Amendment) Bill, 2024**, which is popularly referred to as the **UMEED Act**, was introduced in the **Lok Sabha** on **August 8, 2024**.
 
• The acronym **UMEED** stands for **Unified Waqf Management, Empowerment, Efficiency and Development**. This name reflects the government's objective to modernize and streamline the administration of Waqf properties in **India**.
 
• The bill was introduced by **Kiren Rijiju**, the Union Minister of **Minority Affairs**, aiming to amend the existing **Waqf Act, 1995**, which had been criticized for lacking transparency and accountability.
 
• One of the primary **features** of the **UMEED Act** is the mandatory **registration** of all Waqf properties on a **centralized portal** to ensure better monitoring and prevent illegal encroachments.
 
• The act proposes significant changes to the composition of the **State Waqf Boards** and the **Central Waqf Council**, including the mandatory representation of **two women** and **two non-Muslim** members to ensure a more inclusive administrative structure.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Historical Context of Waqf Laws:**
 
 
• The first major legislation was the **Waqf Act, 1954**, which was later replaced by the more comprehensive **Waqf Act, 1995**.
 
• In **2013**, the **United Progressive Alliance (UPA)** government introduced amendments to provide more powers to the Waqf Boards, but the current **2024-2025** amendment seeks to balance these powers with **government oversight**.
 
 
 
• **Definition of Waqf:**
 
 
• **Waqf** refers to the permanent dedication of movable or immovable **property** for purposes recognized by **Muslim Law** as pious, religious, or charitable.
 
• The person making such a dedication is known as a **Wakif**, and the manager of the property is called a **Mutawalli**.
 
 
 
• **Central Waqf Council:**
 
 
• It is a **statutory body** established in **1964** by the **Government of India** under the original Act.
 
• Its **function** is to advise the Union Government on matters concerning the working of **State Waqf Boards** and the due administration of Waqf properties in the **country**.
 
 
 
• **Waqf-al-Aulad:**
 
 
• This refers to a **Waqf** created for the maintenance and support of the donor's own **family** and descendants. The **UMEED Act** seeks to bring more clarity to the rights of women in such family-based endowments.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Role of the District Collector:** Under the **Waqf (Amendment) Bill, 2024**, the power to conduct a **survey** of Waqf properties and decide whether a property is "Waqf" or "Government land" has been transferred from the **Survey Commissioner** to the **District Collector**.
 
• **Removal of 'Waqf by User':** The new bill proposes to remove the concept of **Waqf by User**, meaning a property cannot be declared as Waqf merely because it has been used for religious purposes for a long **duration**; it now requires a formal **Waqfnama** (deed).
 
• **Financial Audits:** To increase **efficiency** and reduce corruption, the act mandates that the **accounts** of Waqf Boards be audited by the **Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG)** of India or a designated authority.
 
• **Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC):** Following intense debate in **Parliament**, the bill was referred to a **Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC)** consisting of **31 members** (21 from Lok Sabha and 10 from Rajya Sabha) for further scrutiny and stakeholder consultation.
 
• **Data and Scale:** India has the largest **landholding** under Waqf outside the Islamic world, with over **8.7 lakh** registered properties covering approximately **9.4 lakh acres** of land across various **states**.
</ul

questions.question: Who became the first athlete in history to run sub-10 s in the 100 m for 11 consecutive years?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Akani Simbine**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **South African** sprinter **Akani Simbine** made history in **July 2024** by becoming the first athlete to record sub-10 second times in the **100m** for **11 consecutive years**.
 
• He achieved this milestone at the **London Diamond League** held at the **London Stadium**, where he clocked a season-best time of **9.86 seconds**.
 
• This remarkable streak began in **2014** when he first broke the **10-second barrier**, and he has maintained this world-class performance level every single year through **2024**.
 
• By reaching 11 consecutive years, he officially surpassed the previous record of **9 consecutive years** held by the legendary **Jamaican** sprinter **Usain Bolt**, who maintained his streak from **2008 to 2016**. ***Hence, the statement regarding his record-breaking consistency is correct.***
 
• The **Diamond League** performance in **2024** served as a crucial warm-up for the **Paris 2024 Olympics**, reinforcing his status as one of the most consistent sprinters in athletic history. ***Hence, Akani Simbine is the correct answer.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Akani Simbine:**
 
 
• Born on **21 September 1993** in **Johannesburg, South Africa**, Simbine is a specialist in the **100 meters** sprint.
 
• He is the **South African national record holder** in the 100m and has consistently finished in the top 5 at major championships, including the **Tokyo 2020** and **Paris 2024 Olympics**.
 
• His career is defined by extreme consistency, having reached the finals of the **World Athletics Championships** and **Olympic Games** multiple times since **2016**.
 
 
 
• **Usain Bolt:**
 
 
• An **eight-time Olympic gold medalist**, Bolt is the world record holder in the **100m (9.58s)** and **200m (19.19s)**.
 
• While he is considered the greatest sprinter of all time, his streak of sub-10 second finishes lasted **9 years**, ending with his retirement in **2017**.
 
 
 
• **Trayvon Bromell:**
 
 
• An **American** sprinter who was the first high school athlete to break the 10-second barrier.
 
• Although he has recorded extremely fast times, including a personal best of **9.76 seconds**, his career has been plagued by **Achilles tendon injuries**, preventing a long consecutive yearly streak.
 
 
 
• **Andre De Grasse:**
 
 
• A **Canadian** sprinter and the **2020 Olympic 200m champion**.
 
• Known as a "big-game performer," De Grasse has won numerous medals at the **Olympics** and **World Championships**, but his sub-10 second performances in the 100m have not occurred in **11 consecutive years**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **sub-10 second barrier** is a historical hallmark of elite sprinting. While many athletes have achieved it, maintaining the physical condition to do so annually for over a decade is rare due to the high risk of **injuries** and **age-related** physiological declines.
 
• **Asafa Powell**, another **Jamaican** legend, holds the record for the **most total sub-10 second clockings** in history (97 times), but Simbine’s record focuses on the **consecutive nature** of the years in which the feat was achieved.
 
• The **World Athletics** governing body tracks these statistics to highlight longevity in the sport, where **Akani Simbine** now stands as the benchmark for sustained excellence in the **100m dash**.
 
• Simbine's 2024 season also saw him anchor the **South African 4x100m relay team** to a **Silver Medal** at the **Paris 2024 Olympics**, further cementing his legacy in **African athletics**.

questions.question: Which telemedicine platform served over 36 crore patients by April 2025, per the Ministry of Health?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**eSanjeevani**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **eSanjeevani** is the **National Telemedicine Service** of India, designed to provide online medical consultations to citizens across the **country**.
 
• By **April 2025**, the platform achieved a significant milestone by serving over **36 crore** patients, as reported by the **Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW)**.
 
• It was conceptualized to implement **Ayushman Bharat**'s mandate of providing health and wellness services digitally, ensuring that **rural** and **remote areas** have access to quality healthcare.
 
• The platform operates through two primary modes: **eSanjeevaniAB-HWC** (provider-to-provider) and **eSanjeevaniOPD** (patient-to-doctor), facilitating a wide range of medical advice from **general medicine** to **specialized care**.
 
• This initiative has been instrumental in reducing the **out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE)** for patients by eliminating the need for long-distance travel to reach **tertiary care hospitals**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **eSanjeevaniAB-HWC:**
 
 
• This is a **doctor-to-doctor** telemedicine system launched in **November 2019**.
 
• It connects **Health and Wellness Centres (HWCs)** at the village level with **Hubs** located at **District Hospitals** or **Medical Colleges**.
 
• This model ensures that patients at the **grassroots level** can consult with **specialists** without leaving their locality.
 
 
 
• **eSanjeevaniOPD:**
 
 
• Launched during the **COVID-19 pandemic** in **April 2020**, this variant allows **patients** to consult doctors directly from their **homes** using a **smartphone** or **laptop**.
 
• It features **video consultations**, **online prescriptions**, and **SMS notifications**, making it a highly **user-friendly** application for the general public.
